title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Aviation
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Two more airlines lose customer data through IT suppliers in one week: card-skimming code on Norwegian’s booking sites and 618,000 airBaltic bookings exposed
items.content_text: Norwegian Air confirmed on 19 November that attackers who breached one of its external IT suppliers placed malicious code on parts of its booking websites on 16 November, where it captured card numbers, expiry dates and security codes. About 5,000 customers in Norway and Sweden were told to block their cards. Norwegian says its internal systems, servers and app were not compromised and it has reported the incident to Norway’s data protection authority; Cybernews reports that around 200 companies may be affected through the same supplier, which has not been named. Four days earlier, on 15 November, airBaltic said an unnamed external IT provider had exposed about 618,000 bookings made online between 18 July and 12 November: names, booking references and flight details, but not payment or travel-document data. It suspended online check-in and booking management for the roughly 11,800 affected bookings with flights still to come; flights ran normally. Both follow the widening Amadeus reservation-data breach (see Incidents & Attacks). None of these touched flight operations or OT, and they do not count as OT attacks in this page’s threat level; they lead because they are the newest confirmed attacks on aviation operators. Our assessment: airlines and airports increasingly share the same few suppliers for booking, check-in, departure control and baggage, so a supplier’s weakest account is the operator’s exposure.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Cybernews and TV4/TT (Norwegian); ERR and Migflug (airBaltic, citing the airline’s statement)

items.title: The FAA’s nationwide ground stop traced to data flooding its telecom network during a router deployment — the FAA says it has no indication of a cyberattack
items.content_text: The FAA halted departures at every US airport from about 3:30 PM ET on 13 November after its legacy air traffic systems became unstable at 17 of 22 en-route centres and then several approach controls. Its 15 November update says data began flooding the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure network, about 1,000 connection attempts every 4–5 seconds, traced initially to a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas, where provider L3Harris was deploying a new router. Blocking both sites stabilised the network and traffic resumed at 8:15 PM ET; about 12,462 flights were cancelled in the aftermath. The FAA says it has “no indication that this was a cyberattack” and the root-cause investigation continues. The lesson: one network change can stop safety-critical operations nationwide (editorial assessment).

items.title: A United Airlines system outage left crews without final weight-and-balance figures, holding mainline departures three days after the FAA ground stop
items.content_text: On the afternoon of 16 November United Airlines reported a “widespread system outage” that stopped final weight-and-balance and takeoff-performance data reaching crews, so mainline departures could not leave the gate. A pilots’ union memo described a company-wide, web-based outage affecting several pilot applications, including crew communications; at Chicago O’Hare the pushback-request system also went down. Crews reported problems from about 4:02 PM ET and some received final weights between 4:40 and 5:09 PM. FlightAware counted 418 United flights delayed and 21 cancelled that day from all causes; aircraft already airborne and United Express were unaffected. United says there is “no indication that this is a cybersecurity-related issue” and has not named the failed system. The lesson: dispatch-to-cockpit data paths are operational systems and need a practised manual fallback (editorial assessment).

items.title: The Amadeus breach widens: Cathay Pacific, ANA, Malaysia Airlines and Condor join JAL, Korean Air and Asiana, and Amadeus says it has fixed the vulnerability
items.content_text: Amadeus said in early November that “certain booking-display data was accessible through the vulnerability”, that it has fixed the flaw and strengthened monitoring, and that it has found no sign of payment-data access or ransomware. Cathay Pacific disclosed on 30 October that about 53,000 bookings were reached using Amadeus system-account credentials between August 2023 and September 2026: mostly names, booking references and itineraries, a smaller set with contact, travel-document or frequent-flyer details. ANA reports up to 37,800 passengers, Malaysia Airlines says data processed through Amadeus in that window may be affected, and Condor says its data was affected. JAL (about 92,000 customers), Korean Air and Asiana disclosed in late October. No actor is named and no airline reports operational impact. This is an IT and data incident, not an OT one (editorial assessment).

items.title: CISA and FBI warn of an ongoing threat to internet-connected refrigeration controllers, naming transport and cold storage alongside food retail
items.content_text: Attackers tampered with internet-connected refrigeration controllers at hundreds of French supermarkets in October and, in a second wave on 1–2 November, in about 11 European countries, forcing units into continuous heating or defrost; three French blood-service sites also had settings changed. On 5 November CISA and the FBI, with HHS, USDA and DOT, warned that the threat is ongoing and also reaches healthcare, chemical, transport and cold-storage operations. France attributes the October attack to Iran’s IRGC, which Iran denies. Sweden’s NCSC says victims mainly ran older systems with weak passwords, and Sekoia says the second wave used a non-public flaw that renames the controller’s admin account. No airport or airline victim is reported. Airport cargo cold rooms for pharmaceuticals and airline catering units run similar controllers (editorial assessment).

items.title: Norway says intruders reached Equinor and Skagerak through Microsoft’s Azure API Management, a cloud layer that also links airline and airport systems
items.content_text: On 23 November Norway’s National Security Authority (NSM) said an unidentified actor has been stealing access tokens and other sensitive data from Microsoft Azure API Management (APIM), and that energy companies Equinor and Skagerak Energi were among those hit. Equinor detected its intrusion on 17 November and contained it by 20 November; both firms say production carried on normally, and NSM found no service disruption. A reported, non-public Microsoft notice says an issue in older “Classic” APIM tiers was found on 18 November and closed the next day; Microsoft has issued credential-rotation guidance but has not publicly linked it to Norway. No aviation organisation is named. Airlines and airports that publish booking, check-in, flight-status or ground-handling APIs through APIM should rotate those secrets now (editorial assessment).

items.title: Suspected GPS jamming over the North Sea degrades navigation for about 80 aircraft, and seven have RNP approach problems into Schiphol
items.content_text: On 9 November dozens of aircraft over the Netherlands, the North Sea and nearby airspace lost or degraded GPS, GPS World reported on 16 November, citing Aviation24.be. Seven aircraft had problems with their Required Navigation Performance systems on approach to Amsterdam Schiphol and landed safely with help from air traffic controllers; Dutch air traffic control considers deliberate jamming plausible. ADS-B analysis by John Wiseman suggests about 80 aircraft were affected over roughly 20 minutes and points to a possible source near sea level north of Texel, where several Russian-flagged vessels were reportedly present; that link is not confirmed. EASA’s July bulletin says jamming and spoofing have grown in frequency and sophistication since February 2022. This is radio interference, not a cyber compromise, but it hits navigation directly (editorial assessment).

items.title: DHS tells Congress Iran-backed hackers have stepped up attacks on US transportation, water and energy, while officials rule out hacking in the FAA ground stop
items.content_text: In written testimony for a House Homeland Security Committee hearing on 18 November, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Iranian state-sponsored groups and pro-Iranian criminals have targeted US critical infrastructure since the conflict with Iran began in February, with transportation, healthcare, water, energy and financial services increasingly in their sights. He described most attacks so far as localized, low-damage disruptions of poorly secured industrial control systems. At the same hearing the Director of National Intelligence and DHS said they found no evidence that hackers caused the nationwide FAA ground stop, the Microsoft 365 outage or other recent disruptions. AttackIQ research released on 17 November describes Iranian groups handing access to one another and reaching targets through contractors and suppliers. No aviation victim is named; exposed airport controllers fit the profile (editorial assessment).

items.title: A vCenter authentication bypass was exploited as a zero-day for two months before Broadcom’s 19 November patch — and vCenter 7.0 gets no fix
items.content_text: Broadcom patched CVE-2026-123890 on 19 November, a critical flaw in vCenter’s directory service that lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker obtain an administrator session; CISA added it to KEV on 20 November. Google’s Mandiant says a suspected China-linked espionage group it tracks as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) exploited it for more than two months, getting in through a BeyondTrust Remote Support flaw, attacking vCenter in early September, stealing SAML signing material and the vCenter master key, and moving on to ESXi hosts. Fixes are in vCenter 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200 and 8.0 U3m; end-of-life 7.0 has no public patch. No victims or sectors are named. Airport baggage-control, BMS and flight-information servers often run as virtual machines, so whoever holds vCenter holds them (editorial assessment).

items.title: Dragos counts 1,266 ransomware attacks on industrial organizations in Q3, with transport and logistics third, and no case of an operator touching a control system
items.content_text: Dragos said on 16 November that ransomware hit 1,266 industrial organizations between July and September 2026, up 11% on the second quarter, while the number of brands claiming industrial victims rose from 70 to 99. Manufacturing took 69% of cases, followed by the ICS ecosystem of integrators, engineering firms and equipment makers (116) and transport and logistics (105). Dragos saw no Q3 case of a ransomware operator manipulating a control system: operations stopped because the IT, ERP and virtualization layers they rely on went down. Entry came through edge devices and enterprise applications exploited within days of disclosure, and through stolen VPN and firewall credentials. The same pattern applies at airports: baggage, fuelling and ground operations stop when the servers and identity systems behind them fail (editorial assessment).

items.title: Lumen exposes Volt Typhoon’s “Silent Train” relay network and lists aviation among the critical-infrastructure sectors where the group has had victims
items.content_text: Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs published research on 28 October describing “Silent Train”, the covert access framework it says the China-linked group Volt Typhoon has used since November 2023: rotating, per-target chains of compromised home-office routers, IoT devices and enterprise equipment that CyberScoop says can be assembled in under two minutes. Lumen ties it to campaigns against Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN (CVE-2026-20127), VeloCloud Orchestrator (CVE-2026-16812), N-able N-central (CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876), Versa Director and, with moderate confidence, Quest KACE; all four CVEs are in KEV. It lists aviation among sectors with victims but names no victim, gives no count by sector and describes no OT access. Airports and airlines often link remote navaid sites, fuel farms and regional stations through exactly these platforms (editorial assessment).

items.title: Intel 471: manufacturers, from aerospace to chemicals, are the most-targeted ransomware victims of 2026, and access to them is sold through VPNs and remote access
items.content_text: Intel 471 said on 18 November that manufacturing was the sector most often named by ransomware and extortion groups between January and October 2026, with 1,379 claims, or 16.8% of the victims it tracked. Initial access brokers offered entry to 172 manufacturing organizations, about 10% of all accesses advertised, and perimeter remote access dominated the listings, with VPN access the largest single type at 28.5%. Qilin, The Gentlemen and Akira were the most active groups named. The figures are Intel 471’s own tracking and are not independently verified. The report covers aerospace manufacturers, and the same parts suppliers, MRO shops and component makers feed airline maintenance and airport projects, so a stolen supplier VPN login is an aviation supply-chain risk (editorial assessment).

items.title: Trellix counts a 50.8% jump in ransomware leak-site posts against industrial sectors, but finds edge-device break-ins did not reach control networks
items.content_text: Trellix’s November 2026 OT Threat Report, covering April to September, counts about 1,500 ransomware leak-site posts naming organizations in manufacturing, construction, transportation and warehousing, mining and oil and gas extraction, and utilities, up 50.8% on the previous quarter. Manufacturing accounted for about two-thirds; The Gentlemen and Qilin each made up about 16% of posts. In Trellix’s own product telemetry, which measures detection activity rather than compromises, transportation and shipping and aerospace and defense each accounted for 3.7%. Trellix says the enterprise-edge exploitation it tracked did not establish a path into ICS networks. For airports and airlines the message matches Dragos: the disruption comes from losing the IT and identity layers that ground systems depend on (editorial assessment).

items.title: Attackers rooted unpatched Check Point gateways through PHP2Shell, planted backdoors and wiped a VMware host — the root flaw is now in KEV
items.content_text: Check Point Research said on 12 November that attackers exploited the PHP2Shell flaws on unpatched Check Point Mobile Access portals from 30 October, then used a local flaw, CVE-2026-123039, to become root. They planted backdoors, pivoted to a VMware ESXi host and ran a wiper. The first wave hit Israeli organizations, some destructively; a second wave from 2 November reached several countries without destruction. Attribution is unconfirmed, though the tooling resembles that of the China-nexus group UNC5221. CISA added the root flaw to KEV on 13 November. No OT or aviation victim is reported, but these gateways often front remote access for airport and airline operations staff and integrators, and ESXi often hosts operational servers (editorial assessment).

items.title: PHP2Shell reaches building automation: CISA publishes a Siemens building-automation and energy advisory as ABB, Schneider and Siemens list affected products, several with no fix
items.content_text: The PHP2Shell flaws (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), unauthenticated code-execution bugs in the PHP runtime disclosed on 21 October, are now confirmed in OT and building products. On 12 November CISA published ICSA-26-316-01, Siemens Building Automation and Energy Products, covering PHP2Shell, alongside a separate advisory for Siemens Desigo and Gridscale; Siemens recommends restricting network access to affected devices. ABB lists its ASPECT building-management gateways and Netcontrol RTUs, Schneider a Foxboro DCS server, and Siemens added WTV676/WTV776 metering gateways on 16 November; several have no fix yet. Palo Alto’s Unit 42 verified that a suspected China-nexus actor used PHP2Shell to root about two dozen PAN-OS firewalls in late October. No OT product is reported exploited. Terminal buildings commonly run building controllers of this class (editorial assessment).

items.title: Java4Shell exploitation attempts begin, and Siemens tells customers to take Industrial Edge Management offline until patched
items.content_text: Probing for Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a memory-corruption bug in how OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later decode Base64 data, began within two days of its 17 November disclosure. GreyNoise counted more than 150 matching requests from five addresses by early 19 November and Previdian logged nine attempts from six addresses; none is confirmed to have succeeded. Exploitation needs a recent Intel or AMD processor with AVX-512 VBMI, and researchers at Calif showed unauthenticated code execution against default Jira, Confluence, Jenkins and Keycloak set-ups. Siemens advisory SSA-272816 lists three Industrial Edge Management products, with fixes in progress, and recommends taking those instances offline until patched. Cisco lists more than a dozen unfixed products. Java runs inside many airport operations and maintenance platforms (editorial assessment).

items.title: N-able ships Hotfix 3 for 17 more N-central flaws after attackers planted miners on servers already running Hotfix 2
items.content_text: N-able released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 3 on 16 November as a critical security update. It fixes 17 new CVEs, including authentication bypasses, path traversal leading to code execution and a syslog injection that runs commands as root, and removes the Legacy API option that the exploited 4EverAble2Shell chain depends on. On-premises servers need the upgrade now; hosted servers update automatically, but every customer must also upgrade Agents and Probes, which N-able warns can otherwise be impersonated. The fix follows Huntback’s 13 November finding of cryptocurrency miners on 21 N-central servers, 19 of them on Hotfix 2. Separately, on 20 November N-able said attackers reached a server in its hosted Mail Assure and SpamExperts email-filtering cloud. Integrators often manage airport and airline Windows hosts through RMM tools (editorial assessment).

items.title: Attackers root clustered Cisco Expressway gateways soon after a public exploit, and CISA adds the flaw to KEV
items.content_text: Security firm F6 says attackers exploited CVE-2026-76466, a critical flaw in clustered Cisco Expressway Core and Edge deployments, shortly after proof-of-concept code appeared on GitHub. They broke into two internet-facing Expressway nodes at an unnamed Russian organization, moved to two more cluster nodes inside the network and gained root, then ran Python scripts that F6 says show signs of AI-assisted writing to scan for SMB shares, SQL Server and WinRM hosts and to search GitLab for credentials. CISA added the flaw to KEV on 20 November. Cisco disclosed and fixed it on 21 October; there is no workaround. No OT victim is reported. Expressway often links outside callers, including vendors and remote operations centres, into internal networks (editorial assessment).

items.title: Attackers exploit a CVSS 10 Node-RED flaw on Siemens SIMATIC IoT2050 gateways to plant botnet malware and persistent backdoors
items.content_text: VulnCheck has seen exploitation attempts since 30 October against CVE-2026-58115 (CVSS 10.0), missing authentication in the Node-RED HTTP interface on Siemens SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices running Industrial OS with Node-RED installed, The Hacker News reported on 3 November. An unauthenticated attacker can create Node-RED flows that run code with full privileges. Attempts deployed flows that downloaded a Linux botnet binary, later moved to a two-stage loader, and in some cases created an HTTP endpoint that passes commands to an exec node, a backdoor that survives reboots. Siemens advisory SSA-834709 fixes it in Node-RED 4.3.4.1 and recommends uninstalling Node-RED where it is not needed. No victims are named. IoT2050-class gateways often collect data from building, energy and equipment monitoring (editorial assessment).

items.title: A Brotli flaw already in CISA’s exploited list reaches Siemens WinCC and WinCC OA, and most products have no fix yet
items.content_text: Siemens says CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write in the widely used Brotli compression decoder, affects several of its industrial software lines, and CISA republished the assessment as an ICS advisory on 17 November. The bug can crash the software, leak information or possibly allow code execution. CISA added the CVE to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 27 October because of attacks on other software; nobody has reported exploitation through a Siemens product. Affected products include WinCC OA V3.20 and V3.21, WinCC Runtime Professional, WinCC V7/V8, TIA Administrator and BRAUMAT/SISTAR. Fixes exist only for WinCC OA V3.20 (P17.1) and BRAUMAT/SISTAR, so most sites must rely on the workaround. WinCC and WinCC OA are common supervisory software for airport building, energy, conveyor and tunnel systems, which is why this cross-sector advisory is carried here (editorial assessment).

items.title: CISA’s 2030 strategy puts operational technology and consequence-based priorities at the centre — a review of its core services starts within 60 days
items.content_text: CISA released “CISA 2030: Defend, Harden, Prevail” on 26 October. Acting Director Nick Andersen says the agency will move from passive defence to an aggressive, anticipatory stance that removes adversary footholds, with resilience as the foundation. The plan commits CISA to helping operators improve OT security, including asset visibility and intrusion detection; to producing data-driven guidance on third-party and supply-chain dependencies; and to helping sectors focus resources where they have the greatest impact, including through a national risk register on the UK model. It sets three timelines: a review of core services and capabilities beginning within 60 days, an implementation plan with success metrics within 180 days, and a progress update after a year. It places no new obligations on operators, and Cybersecurity Dive notes that it does not address the agency’s shrinking field presence after workforce cuts. Aviation is not named. For airports and airlines the relevance is direction of travel: federal attention and services are being steered toward OT visibility, detection and the most consequential assets, the same case that terminal and airfield OT programmes make internally.
tags: Regulation & Policy — CISA four-year strategy; no new obligations for operators
